title: Structure of Atom
tagline: From cathode rays to quantum numbers: how the electron cloud of an atom was discovered, modelled and mapped.

overview.intro: The second unit traces one of the most successful lines of reasoning in science: the discovery of the particles inside the atom and the successive models built to explain their behaviour. You will follow the experiments that revealed the electron, the proton and the neutron, the Rutherford scattering experiment that replaced the plum-pudding model with a nuclear atom, and the failures of classical physics that led Bohr to quantise the electron's energy. The unit then moves to the quantum mechanical model, where orbitals defined by four quantum numbers replace fixed orbits, and to the calculations that connect wavelength, frequency and energy in the spectra of hydrogen.

learningOutcomes: Describe the experiments that discovered the electron, proton and neutron and state what each showed about atomic structure.
Compare the Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models and explain why each earlier model failed.
Apply the photoelectric equation, the Bohr radius and energy relations, and the Rydberg equation to numerical problems.
Write electronic configurations using Aufbau, Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle, and derive the four quantum numbers of an electron.

blocks.text: The electron was discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897 while studying cathode rays — streams of particles emitted from the cathode in a partially evacuated discharge tube. The rays originate at the cathode, travel in straight lines, produce a fluorescence where they strike the glass, and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields. Because they bend towards the positive plate, the particles carry a negative charge. Making the deflection equal in electric and magnetic fields gave the charge-to-mass ratio e/m = 1.759 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹, the same value whatever the cathode material or the gas in the tube — proof that the electron is a constituent of every atom, not a property of one element. Robert Millikan's oil-drop experiment of 1909 then showed that charge is quantised: every drop carried a whole multiple of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so the electron's charge is that value and its mass is 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

Alpha particles emitted by radioactive radium were used by Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden in 1911 to probe the atom. A beam of alpha particles was fired at a thin gold foil: most passed straight through, a small fraction was deflected through large angles, and about 1 in 8000 bounced back almost backwards. Rutherford concluded that the atom is mostly empty space, with nearly all its mass and all its positive charge concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus of a few femtometres; the electrons occupy the rest of the volume. The nuclear model explained the scattering but not the stability of atoms: a charged particle accelerating in a spiral towards the nucleus should radiate energy continuously, which classical electrodynamics predicted but which is never observed.

Two further particles completed the picture. The proton was identified by Rutherford in 1919 when alpha particles knocked hydrogen nuclei out of nitrogen gas, showing that the hydrogen nucleus is a constituent of all nuclei; it carries +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and has a mass of 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, about 1836 times the electron mass. The neutron was postulated by Rutherford in 1920 to explain why atomic masses exceed the sum of proton masses, and was finally discovered by Chadwick in 1932 when beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles and highly penetrating neutral radiation was emitted. The neutron carries no charge and has a mass of 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, slightly greater than the proton mass. Together they give the notation for an isotope ᴬ𝑍X, where Z is the atomic number (protons) and A is the mass number (protons plus neutrons).

learn.title: Atomic models: from Thomson to Bohr

blocks.text: Thomson's model, proposed in 1904, pictured the atom as a sphere of uniform positive charge with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding or seeds in a watermelon, so that the atom as a whole is neutral. It explained electrical neutrality and the emission of electrons as ions, but it could not explain the large-angle scattering of alpha particles, because a diffuse positive charge has no concentrated field strong enough to repel an alpha particle backwards. The model was replaced by Rutherford's nuclear atom, which described the scattering correctly but, being a classical model, predicted that an orbiting electron would radiate energy continuously, spiral into the nucleus and collapse the atom in about 10⁻¹¹ s. Since matter is stable, classical physics had to be amended.

Bohr's model (1913) rescued the nuclear atom by adding two quantum postulates. First, electrons revolve around the nucleus only in certain allowed circular orbits called stationary states, and an electron in such an orbit radiates no energy despite being accelerated. Second, the angular momentum of the electron in an allowed orbit is an integral multiple of h/2π, where h is Planck's constant; this gives the radius of the nth orbit as rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z ångström for hydrogen-like species. The energy of an electron in the nth orbit is Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV, so the energy is quantised and negative because the electron is bound. Radiation is emitted only when an electron jumps from a higher energy level to a lower one, with the energy of the photon equal to the difference between the levels: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν.

Bohr's model succeeded for hydrogen but failed for helium and heavier atoms, and it could not explain the fine structure of spectral lines or why atoms give sharp lines at all. Two experiments forced the abandonment of the idea of a definite electron path. In 1924 de Broglie proposed that matter has a wave nature, with a wavelength λ = h/mv; an electron in the first Bohr orbit has a circumference exactly equal to one wavelength, so the allowed orbits are those that fit a whole number of waves. In 1927 Heisenberg's uncertainty principle stated that it is impossible to determine simultaneously both the position and the momentum of an electron with arbitrary accuracy: Δx × Δp ≥ h/4π. Because the electron has no well-defined orbit, the quantum mechanical model replaces it with a wave function ψ whose square, |ψ|², gives the probability of finding the electron in a small volume — an orbital is the region where there is a 90% probability of finding the electron, not a path.

Schrödinger's wave equation of 1926 yields solutions called orbitals, each specified by three quantum numbers plus spin. The principal quantum number n is a positive integer that determines the size and energy of the orbital and the main shell; the azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number l has integer values from 0 to n−1 and determines the shape, with l = 0, 1, 2 and 3 corresponding to the s, p, d and f subshells; the magnetic quantum number mₗ runs from −l to +l and determines the orientation of the orbital in space; and the spin quantum number mₛ is +½ or −½, representing the two possible orientations of the electron's spin. The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. The s orbital is spherical, the p orbital is dumbbell-shaped along one axis, and the d orbitals are double-dumbbell shaped.

learn.title: Bohr model of hydrogen and the hydrogen spectrum

blocks.text: A hydrogen discharge tube gives a line spectrum rather than a continuous band because only certain energies are emitted. Bohr's equations reproduce it quantitatively: the radius of the nth orbit is rₙ = n² × 0.529 Å, the energy is Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, and the wave number of an emitted line is 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where R is the Rydberg constant, 109,677 cm⁻¹. Transitions from higher levels down to n = 1 form the ultraviolet Lyman series; transitions ending at n = 2 form the visible Balmer series with lines at 656, 486, 434 and 410 nm; and transitions to n = 3, 4 and 5 form the infrared Pfund, Brackett and Humphreys series. Because the energy levels converge as n increases, the lines of a series crowd together towards the series limit.

items.text: Calculate the radius and energy of the electron in the second orbit of a hydrogen atom.
Find the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series (n₂ = 3 → n₁ = 2).
Calculate the ionisation energy of hydrogen from its ionisation potential of 13.6 eV.
items.note: Ionisation means n = 1 → n = ∞, so ΔE = 0 − (−13.6) = 13.6 eV per atom = 13.6 × 96.49 kJ mol⁻¹ = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ (or 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 13.6 = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom).

items: The photoelectric effect showed that light behaves as packets (photons) of energy E = hν = hc/λ, with the kinetic energy of the ejected electron equal to hν minus the work function.
The threshold frequency ν₀ is the minimum frequency that ejects electrons; below it, no electrons are emitted however intense the light.
Spectral analysis is chemical analysis: each element has its own set of spectral lines, used to identify elements in stars and in the laboratory.
Energy level diagram: energy increases upwards, the gap between levels decreases as n rises, and emission is drawn as a downward arrow while absorption is an upward arrow.

keyPoints: Thomson discovered the electron (1897); Millikan measured its charge (1909); Rutherford identified the proton (1919); Chadwick found the neutron (1932).
Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed the atom is mostly empty space with a small dense nucleus containing nearly all the mass.
Classical physics predicted the nuclear atom would collapse; Bohr saved it by quantising the allowed orbits.
Bohr: rₙ = 0.529 n² Å and Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV for hydrogen-like atoms.
Emission occurs when an electron falls to a lower level, with hν equal to the energy difference between the levels.
de Broglie: λ = h/mv; Heisenberg: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π — together they rule out fixed orbits.
An orbital is a 90% probability region described by |ψ|², not an electron path.
Quantum numbers n, l, mₗ and mₛ fix the shell, shape, orientation and spin of an electron.
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons may share an identical set of four quantum numbers.
The Rydberg equation 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) reproduces every line of the hydrogen spectrum.
examFocus: Expect numerical application: ionisation energy, radius of an orbit, wavelength of a spectral line and the threshold-frequency photoelectric equation are all "applying" questions worth 2-3 marks each.
Definitions of the sub-atomic particles with their charges and masses, and comparisons of the three atomic models, are standard short-answer material.
Writing electronic configurations and deriving sets of quantum numbers regularly appears as a short or analytical answer; always state n, l, mₗ and mₛ explicitly.

A number that fixes an electron's shell, subshell, orbital orientation or spin.
The emission of electrons from a metal when light of sufficient frequency strikes it.
R = 109,677 cm⁻¹, the constant in the wave-number expression for the hydrogen spectrum.
Heisenberg's relation Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, which forbids simultaneous exact position and momentum.
The energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
A set of spectral lines produced by transitions ending at the same lower energy level.

questions.prompt: The discovery of the neutron by Chadwick in 1932 explained why:
options: atomic masses exceed the sum of proton masses
questions.answer: atomic masses exceed the sum of proton masses
questions.explanation: Atoms contain electrons and protons whose masses sum to less than the measured nuclear mass. The uncharged neutron fills the gap, adding mass without changing the atomic number Z, so option A is correct.

questions.prompt: The number of angular momentum quantum numbers possible for an electron in the 3d subshell is:
questions.explanation: For a d subshell l = 2, and mₗ takes values from −l to +l, giving −2, −1, 0, +1 and +2 — five values, one for each of the five d orbitals.

questions.prompt: The wavelength of the light emitted in the transition from n = 3 to n = 2 in hydrogen is about:
questions.explanation: A transition ending at n = 2 belongs to the Balmer series and the n = 3 → n = 2 line is Hα at 656.5 nm, the red line of the hydrogen spectrum. 486 nm is Hβ (n = 4 → 2) and 122 nm lies in the ultraviolet Lyman series.

questions.prompt: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential of 100 V is approximately:
questions.explanation: The electron gains kinetic energy eV, so p = √(2meV) = √(2 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 100) = 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. Then λ = h/p = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 123 pm, which matches the standard shortcut λ = 1227/√V pm = 1227/10 = 123 pm.

questions.prompt: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is __________.
questions.explanation: The Bohr radius is a₀ = 0.529 ångström (5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m); since rₙ scales as n², the radius of orbit n is 0.529 n² Å.

questions.prompt: The energy of an electron in the n = 2 orbit of hydrogen is __________.
questions.explanation: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV per atom, i.e. −328 kJ mol⁻¹. The negative sign shows the electron is bound to the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Why did Rutherford's nuclear model fail to explain the stability of atoms?
questions.answer: In Rutherford's model the electron orbits the nucleus under electrostatic attraction. Classical electrodynamics says an accelerated charge radiates energy continuously, so the electron would lose energy, spiral inward and collapse into the nucleus in about 10⁻¹¹ s, making the atom unstable. Matter is stable, so the model — which predicted continuous radiation instead of sharp spectral lines — had to be replaced by Bohr's quantised model.
questions.explanation: This is the classic reasoning question on atomic models: the classical prediction of continuous radiation and a spiral collapse is contradicted by the sharp line spectrum that is actually observed.

questions.prompt: State the Pauli exclusion principle and apply it to the 2p subshell.
questions.answer: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so each orbital accommodates a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins. For the 2p subshell n = 2 and l = 1, giving three orbitals (mₗ = −1, 0, +1); each holds two electrons of opposite spin, so the 2p subshell holds a maximum of six electrons with sets such as (2, 1, −1, +½), (2, 1, −1, −½), (2, 1, 0, +½) and so on.
questions.explanation: Each of the four quantum numbers must be quoted for the electrons: the subshell holds six electrons because the three p orbitals each accommodate a pair of opposite spin.

questions.prompt: Explain the photoelectric effect and calculate the maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected from a metal of work function 4.2 eV by light of wavelength 250 nm.
questions.answer: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal when light of sufficient frequency strikes it. Photons of energy E = hν = hc/λ are absorbed; if this exceeds the work function φ, the extra energy appears as kinetic energy of the ejected electron, and below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted however intense the light. E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(250 × 10⁻⁹) = 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 4.97 eV. KE(max) = 4.97 − 4.2 = 0.77 eV per electron, equal to 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: Photoelectric questions are solved in two steps: convert the wavelength to photon energy in eV, then subtract the work function to leave the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron.

questions.prompt: Write the electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) and explain why it differs from the prediction of the Aufbau principle, stating how Hund's rule and exchange energy relate to it.
questions.answer: The Aufbau prediction is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁴, but the observed configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹. A half-filled d subshell with five parallel-spin electrons in five separate orbitals is unusually stable: the symmetrical distribution of charge and the extra exchange energy released by having five like spins lower the energy of the atom more than pairing two electrons in a 3d orbital would cost. Chromium thus promotes one 4s electron into the 3d subshell. The same effect gives copper (Z = 29) the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s², because a completely filled d subshell is likewise stabilised.
questions.explanation: Chromium and copper are the two standard exceptions to the Aufbau filling order, and marks are awarded for naming half-filled and fully filled subshell stability as the cause.
